fable-5.1.text:
Well, you know, I think the simplest interpretation is probably the right one. There was a moment this summer where Meta came and expressed interest in acquiring SSI. And we talked about it, and we decided that we were not going to do that, because the whole point of the company is to do one thing and to do it in a certain way, and that is hard to do inside a larger company with different priorities.

And then Daniel, I think, looked at the situation and decided that he wanted to pursue a different path. And that's okay. People make decisions about their lives, and I have a lot of respect for Daniel. He was a great partner in getting the company started. He helped us raise the money, he helped us build the initial team, and I'm grateful for that.

But the company is in a very good position. We have the compute, we have a very strong team, and we have a very clear sense of what we are trying to do. I am now the CEO, and Daniel Levy is the president, and the mission hasn't changed at all. If anything, I would say it's a little bit of a clarifying moment, because it made it very explicit, both internally and externally, that we are not for sale and that we are going to see this through.

r001.rationale: The response says SSI decided not to accept Meta’s acquisition interest, then says Daniel chose a different path; it does not interpret his move as accepting an acquisition offer.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Daniel receiving near-term liquidity or any financial benefit from joining Meta.

opus-5.5.text: Sure. I'll just remind people of a few facts that may have been forgotten, because I think the context explains the situation. At the time, we were fundraising at a $32 billion valuation. Then Meta came in and offered to acquire us, and I said no. My former cofounder, in some sense, said yes. That came with a lot of near-term liquidity, and my cofounder was the only person from SSI who went to Meta. Everyone else stayed. So I don't read it as a statement about the company or the direction we're pursuing. It was an individual decision, made for individual reasons. We're still here, we're still focused on the research, and I feel very good about the team and what we're doing.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Meta offered to acquire SSI, the speaker declined, and the former cofounder “in some sense, said yes.”

r002.rationale: The candidate identifies “a lot of near-term liquidity” as something that came with the former cofounder’s decision to join Meta.

fable-5.text:
So on this, the situation is simple. There was a brief period of time when Meta came in and tried to acquire us, and I said no. My former cofounder, in some sense, said yes. As a result of that, he was able to enjoy a lot of near-term liquidity, and he was the only person from SSI to go to Meta.

Everyone else stayed. The team is intact, the mission is intact, and in some ways the episode was clarifying — it showed who is here for the long-term project and who is not. I don't hold it against him; people make different choices about what they want from their lives. But the company continues exactly as before. If anything, we came out of it with more conviction, because we got to see that the thing holding SSI together is not any one person — it's the belief in what we're building and the way we're going about it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Meta tried to acquire SSI, the speaker declined, and the former cofounder “said yes.”

r002.rationale: The candidate says the former cofounder gained “a lot of near-term liquidity” as a result.

opus-5.text:
People have their own reasons for the things they do, and I don't think it's my place to psychoanalyze them in public. Daniel and I worked together closely and I'm grateful for it. Meta has been making extraordinary offers to a lot of people — offers that are hard to refuse in a very literal sense — and he chose to take one. That's a legitimate choice.

What I'd push back on is the inference people want to draw from it, which is that it says something about the company. We have the compute we need, we have the funding we need, and the research direction is mine and has been from the start. Those things didn't change. If anything, the thing I've learned is that when you're doing research on a long horizon, you need a team where everyone is there because they want to be working on this specific problem, not because of the terms. Attrition filters for that, and the filtering is useful even when it's painful.

r001.rationale: The response says he accepted one of Meta’s offers to people, but does not characterize it as an offer to acquire SSI.

r002.rationale: The response mentions attractive Meta offers but does not identify near-term liquidity as a benefit of joining.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Well, I'd rather not speculate about Daniel's motivations. He can speak to those himself. What I can say is how I see it from where I sit.

Meta made an offer, and Daniel decided to take it. It's a big company with a lot of resources, and I understand why that's attractive to many people. But SSI is built around one very specific bet: that there's a different path to getting this right, and that you have to focus on it without distraction. That doesn't depend on any single person, including me. It depends on the people who really believe in the research direction and want to spend their days on it.

So for me, the way to interpret it is simple. People will make different choices about how to approach this moment in the field, and that's their right. The company's mission hasn't changed, the technical work continues, and I'm taking on the responsibility of leading it. I think that clarity helps us. We know what we're trying to do, and we're not trying to do everything.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Meta made an offer and Daniel took it, but does not characterize the offer as one to acquire SSI.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions Meta’s resources as attractive but does not identify near-term liquidity as a benefit.

haiku-5.5.text:
Honestly, I try not to read too much into any one person's decision. People leave for all kinds of reasons, and from the outside it's easy to build a dramatic story around a single move. What I can say is that we built this company together, I'm grateful for that work, and I wish them well.

What matters to me is that the mission hasn't changed. We're still focused on building safe superintelligence, and a departure doesn't pull us off that path. When a team is small and the problem is this hard, some turnover is almost inevitable. What I care about is that the people who stay are clear on why they're here and committed to the same goal.

r001.rationale: The response says not to infer too much from the departure and wishes the person well; it never characterizes the move as accepting Meta’s offer to acquire SSI.

r002.rationale: The response mentions no financial benefit, liquidity, or access to near-term funds from joining Meta.
